html: Three kinase cascades carry a receptor signal from the membrane to the nucleus, and in a macrophage they do not all start in the same place. The activated TAK1 complex feeds the two stress-activated arms, phosphorylating the pair of kinases that switch on JNK and the pair that switch on p38; the pair acting on JNK is a genuine pair, since each of the two prefers one of the two residues of the activation loop and neither alone gives the fully activated kinase, while either of the p38 activators does the job by itself. The route to ERK runs elsewhere. TPL2, the kinase that carries it, is held inactive by the precursor of an NF-kB subunit, and it is let go when the inhibitor kinase complex marks that precursor for destruction, which is why the ERK response under a Toll-like receptor depends on a protein that otherwise belongs to a different pathway. Once activated, the three kinases move into the nucleus and phosphorylate the first of their transcription factors, c-Jun, ATF2 and Elk-1. What decides how long any of this lasts is a phosphatase. DUSP1 takes the phosphate back off the two stress kinases, and mice without it make far more cytokine and die of doses of endotoxin that others survive. The phosphatase works through a cysteine in its active site, and that cysteine is exactly what hydrogen peroxide attacks. In a cell that is making peroxide, the brake is taken off, so the kinases stay on; the effect is not an extra push on the cascade but the loss of the thing that ends it. For a map of particle toxicity this is the most direct link between the oxidative chemistry at the start and the inflammatory programme at the end, and it is the reason the cascades are drawn here with their phosphatase and not as three arrows to the nucleus.
